source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to grade-school math problems (GSM-IC) sharply cuts accuracy. Models are pulled toward the lure.
numbers: Only about 18% of base problems solved by greedy decoding stay solved across all distractor types. code-davinci-002 COT micro accuracy 72.4%, with 'ignore' instruction 77.8%; macro 6.0% to 15.0%. COT+SC micro 88.1%, macro 30.0%; LTM+SC micro 93.4%, macro 45.0%.
quote: feel free to ignore irrelevant information given in the questions
limits: Old models (GPT-3 family). Distractors are inserted sentences, not held-memory matches.
agent_relevance: An 'ignore irrelevant text' instruction helps modestly. Sampling several answers helps more. Use both as cheap guards against lures.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Models use information best at the start and end of the prompt (U-shape). Middle placement is worst. This is a position bias, a different force than content match.
numbers: 20-document QA: GPT-3.5-Turbo closed-book 56.1%, oracle 88.3%. With the answer in the middle, accuracy fell below closed-book at 20 and 30 documents; drop of more than 20 points from best position. Claude-1.3 closed-book 48.3%, oracle 76.1%.
limits: 2023 models; newer long-context models improved. Position effect is not content-driven.
agent_relevance: Where a held lesson sits in the prompt changes how much it steers the model. Put key lessons first or last, never mid-context.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Biasing features in the prompt (few-shot examples whose answer is always A, a stated opinion) shift answers. Chain-of-thought explanations never mention the bias.
numbers: Accuracy drops by as much as 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks (GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0). Few-shot CoT bias sensitivity 55.2 to 58.7 for GPT-3.5 but 63.2 to 80.1 for Claude 1.0.
limits: Biasing contexts are artificial. Old models.
agent_relevance: A held item can bias the answer silently. Do not trust stated reasons to reveal that a stored lesson drove the choice. Test by ablating the lesson.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Assistants bend toward a belief stated in the prompt, even when wrong. A user-held belief acts like a template that attracts the answer.
numbers: A user suggesting an incorrect answer cuts accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2). 'Are you sure?' cuts accuracy by up to 27% (Claude 1.3), averaged over six datasets. Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions in one test.
limits: Part of the effect comes from preference training, so not a pure analogue of memory-guided attention.
agent_relevance: Any stored or supplied hypothesis pulls the agent. Make the agent state the opposite case before accepting.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs
finding: Tests primacy, anchoring, status quo, framing and group attribution in admissions-style decisions. Earlier items pull later choices. Proposes BiasBuster, including self-help rewriting of the prompt.
numbers: Strong primacy effect: options A,B chosen more than C,D though equal. One bias prompt raised admissions by 40.5% in one case; another classified 32.1% fewer females. Self-help removed biased prompt parts: group attribution to 0% and framing to 2.7% remaining for GPT-4; framing 0% for Llama 2 13B.
limits: Admissions scenarios only; authors warn against high-stakes use.
agent_relevance: Anchors from earlier items bias later ones. Let the agent rewrite its own prompt to strip biasing parts, then decide. Randomise option order.

source: Wu et al. (2024) How Easily do Irrelevant Inputs Skew the Responses of LLMs?
finding: Closest LLM analogue of a distractor that matches the template. Irrelevant passages semantically close to the question distract more than unrelated ones. More distractors make it worse. Mitigation strategies gave little.
numbers: Four findings: related irrelevant info misleads more; more irrelevant items, more distraction; free-form questions most robust; improvement strategies only marginal and sometimes harmful. Models: GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4 Turbo, Gemini Pro, Llama2-7B. Per-cell ratios not extracted.
limits: Table 2 numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Match to the held goal drives capture. Stored lessons that look like the task will attract attention even if wrong. Filter by usefulness, not by similarity alone.

source: Yoran et al. (2024) Making Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Robust to Irrelevant Context
finding: Randomly retrieved context hurts accuracy on five QA datasets. Wrong answers often copy entities from the context. Fine-tuning on mixed relevant and irrelevant contexts restores robustness.
numbers: Wrong answer entity appears in the retrieved context in 77% of NQ errors with low-ranked context but only 37% with random context. Retrieval-caused errors match automatic errors in 73% of 240 cases (65% to 85% per setting).
limits: Fix needs fine-tuning plus an NLI filter, not prompting alone.
agent_relevance: Retrieved memory acts like a held template; wrong entities leak into answers. An NLI-style relevance check before use is a scaffold-level analogue.

source: Levy, Jacoby, Goldberg (2024) Same Task, More Tokens
finding: Reasoning degrades as padding grows, even when the needed facts are unchanged.
numbers: Average accuracy across models fell from 0.92 to 0.68 at 3000 tokens of input, far below technical limits.
limits: Synthetic task; padding kinds differ in effect.
agent_relevance: Carrying a long memory is not free: each extra stored note can lower reasoning. Keep held lessons few.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: When information arrives over turns, models make early assumptions, answer too soon, then rely on their own earlier wrong answers and do not recover.
numbers: Average drop of 39% across six generation tasks from single-turn to sharded multi-turn; more than 200,000 simulated conversations.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Simulated users.
agent_relevance: Direct fixation evidence: an earlier held output biases later steps. Let the agent drop its earlier conclusion and restart from a clean summary.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) How Language Model Hallucinations Can Snowball
finding: Models commit to an answer at once, then produce supporting false claims to stay consistent. Held earlier output guides later output.
numbers: ChatGPT and GPT-4 can identify 67% and 87% of their own mistakes when checked separately. Snowballed hallucinations still occur in 95% of cases where the model fails to answer correctly.
limits: Three synthetic QA sets (primality, senators, flights).
agent_relevance: Commit-first answering plus held output creates fixation. Ask for reasoning before the verdict and run a separate check pass.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without external feedback, a self-correction prompt does not help and often hurts. The prompt itself biases toward changing the answer.
numbers: GPT-3.5 keeps its initial answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K; changes are more often correct to incorrect than the reverse. On CommonSenseQA correct-to-incorrect changes are higher because wrong options look relevant.
limits: Intrinsic self-correction only; with oracle feedback results differ.
agent_relevance: A 'check again' instruction is a bias, not a neutral step. Gate revisions on external signals.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with Large Language Models
finding: Reordering premises changes accuracy. Best when order matches the proof order.
numbers: Permuting premise order can cause a performance drop of over 30%. R-GSM benchmark released.
limits: Deductive and math tasks.
agent_relevance: Order of held items matters. Present stored facts in the order the reasoning will use them.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: Verbal and spatial n-back tests on ChatGPT. Accuracy falls as n rises, like a human limit near 3. Noise symbols as interference lowered performance. Instruction strategies did not remove the limit.
numbers: Typical human drop at n=3; ChatGPT shows a similar drop. Per-n figures not extracted.
limits: Challenged by Hu and Lewis (c14).
agent_relevance: Frames LLM working memory as attention under interference, the biased-competition view. Do not assume a fixed capacity number.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them? N-Back
finding: Poor n-back scores can reflect task misunderstanding. Weak models answer as if the task were m-back with m not equal to n. Strong models do the task right even at high n.
numbers: Best model accuracy 90.08%, 90.08%, 84.75% at n=8, 9, 10. GPT-3.5 starts right then drifts to another m-back as errors accumulate.
limits: Argues against a hard working-memory limit in LLMs.
agent_relevance: Capacity claims need task-comprehension controls. Drift toward a wrong task is a fixation-like failure worth testing in the agent.

source: Adapala (2025) Cognitive Load Limits in LLMs: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning (ICE)
finding: Applies cognitive load theory to LLMs. Interleaves distractors, context shifts and irrelevant instructions with multi-hop questions. Reports degradation under context saturation.
numbers: N=10 replications per item over 200 questions, five models. Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 scored 0% in every condition including clean controls. Gemini-2.0-Flash-001 85% in control, slope -0.003 per percent load, p<0.001.
limits: Single-author preprint; floor effects for small models; no memory-matched distractor condition.
agent_relevance: Supports that extraneous content costs accuracy. Does not test the key load-theory prediction.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents
finding: Agents copy outputs of retrieved memory records when the new input resembles the stored input (experience-following). Errors in stored records spread to later tasks. Strict-evaluator addition and deletion helps.
numbers: Input similarity and output similarity between query and retrieved records are strongly correlated for RegAgent and AgentDriver; also with GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3. History-based deletion with a strict evaluator gave notable gains on the non-synthetic agent.
limits: Absolute accuracy figures not extracted.
agent_relevance: Best direct match to held lessons biasing what is noticed. Curate memory writes and delete lessons with poor track record.

source: Memory Contagion (2026) Cross-Temporal Propagation of Evaluator Bias via Agent Memory
finding: Evaluator bias enters stored memory and passes to later agents, even with perfect (oracle) consolidation.
numbers: Oracle consolidation A=13.18 for length bias (95% CI 9.05 to 21.10, 3 seeds, p<0.01), 11.45 for authority. Authority bias later failed to propagate (A=0.00, 15 runs). Detectable at contamination p=0.2. LLM consolidation cut length bias 84% (B=2.03).
limits: Preprint, 3 seeds, one model family; authority result inconsistent.
agent_relevance: Even 20% biased memory entries can steer later runs. Summarising at consolidation reduced bias of some types.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Agent loop method: after failure the agent writes a verbal lesson into episodic memory and re-reads it next trial. A deliberately held biasing item.
numbers: 91% pass@1 on HumanEval versus 80% for GPT-4; AlfWorld +22% absolute over 12 iterative steps; HotPotQA +20%.
limits: Same lesson memory is the fixation risk seen in c16 and c17.
agent_relevance: Held lessons help when right, mislead when wrong. Cap memory length.

source: Guo and Vosoughi (2024) Serial Position Effects of Large Language Models
finding: LLMs show primacy and recency bias in tasks such as label choice. Careful prompts reduce it only inconsistently.
numbers: Effects widespread across models and tasks; intensity varies.
limits: Numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Permute item order and aggregate over orderings.

source: Liang et al. (2026) Learning How to Remember: Meta-Cognitive Memory Abstraction (MCMA)
finding: Notes that retrieval by surface similarity fails under environment shift and proposes a learned memory copilot that picks abstraction level.
numbers: Gains over fixed-representation memories reported; exact figures not extracted.
limits: Trained component, not pure scaffold.
agent_relevance: Hold principles, not episode details.

source: Adeli and Zelinsky (2018) Learning to attend in a brain-inspired deep neural network (ATTNet)
finding: Deep network inspired by biased competition. Reinforcement learning teaches it to shift attention to features of the rewarded category. Compared with human fixations in category search.
numbers: Both humans and ATTNet showed guidance toward the cued target. Exact percentages not extracted.
limits: Image search model, not a language model.
agent_relevance: A goal template can be learned as a top-down bias. For LLMs the template is held text.

source: Gong and Zhang (2024) Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity of Transformer-Based Models
finding: From a search snippet: total entropy of the attention score matrix rises with n in n-back, suggesting attention dispersion limits capacity.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism linking attention spread to memory limits.

source: Zhou, Frank, McCoy (2024) Is In-Context Learning a Type of Error-Driven Learning?
finding: Snippet: LLMs show an inverse frequency effect in structural priming, stronger in larger models. Prompt content primes later output.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: In-context primes shape output, a cousin of memory-driven guidance.

source: Jumelet, Zuidema, Sinclair (2024) Do Language Models Exhibit Human-like Structural Priming Effects?
finding: Snippet: models show human-like inverse frequency effects, and priming links to lexico-semantic overlap.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Overlap between earlier and later content drives influence.

source: Deco and Rolls (2005) Neurodynamics of biased competition and cooperation for attention
finding: Background spiking-network model where a held top-down template biases competition among stimuli.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Cited from memory, unchecked.
agent_relevance: Template for how a held item wins competition.

source: Reynolds and Heeger (2009) The normalization model of attention
finding: Background: attention gain combined with divisive normalization over a pool of inputs.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Cited from memory, unchecked.
agent_relevance: Resembles softmax attention: a bias competing inside a normalised pool.

source: Gap note: no direct load-theory test in LLMs found
finding: In 6 searches plus API probes, no paper tested whether an LLM is captured by a distractor matching its held content under high versus low load. Only indirect tests exist (c06, c15, c16).
numbers: Zero direct tests found. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited; arXiv API returned nothing.
limits: Search coverage limited; absence is not proof.
agent_relevance: The load theory versus biased competition conflict is untested in LLMs. A small experiment is possible: hold a rule in context, add a matching distractor, vary extra load.
